title: Two Ways of Knowing
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart tells of a fall during a sesshin on Salt Spring Island, when a dog chasing a ball hit the back of Kanho's legs and left Kanho briefly paralyzed after landing on head and neck. Kanho recalls the night spent holding a mala, breathing "this moment, this breath," and quotes Shantideva on whom to blame for pain. At an interfaith panel days later, a pastor's plea to choose Jesus before the second coming leads Kanho to vow to stay behind with those left behind, like Jizo, the Bodhisattva of hell beings. Kanho sets the knowing that has lost street names and the Heart Sutra beside a knowing that holds the Metta Sutra without the words, and closes with three questions: Did I love enough? Did I live fully? Did I learn how to let go?

sentences.text: Falling freely, tears and rain on the garden chisel.
Haiku by Anonymous.
Very prolific writer.
How are you tonight?
I do hope that you are well.
Health is very precious.
We should appreciate deeply being alive, hearing, seeing, breathing.
I am grateful for Tim's invitation to give a talk tonight, and I am very grateful that I am here tonight being able to give this talk.
I am grateful because I came face to face with my false sense of certainty.
Some of you have heard rumors of an accident I experienced about two months ago.
I have received some of your emails inquiring about how I am doing, what happened, and so I thought I would talk about it tonight.
This way we can all stay a little bit closer to what actually happened.
During a Zen sesshin retreat on Salt Spring Island, after the day's activities, I went out for an evening walk with several folks and two dogs.
Nothing to it.
A simple walk down a long driveway to stretch the body, enjoy the balmy evening air, chat, and let the dogs have some exercise.
I was doing exactly that when one of the dogs, in hot pursuit of a ball, went into the back of my legs at warp speed.
It happened very fast.
The feeling was similar to slipping on ice.
I did not even react, put out my hands or anything.
My feet went higher than my body, and so I landed on my head and my upper neck.
My instant reaction of wanting to sit up and checking myself was thwarted by the fact that I was paralyzed.
Except my hands prickled like I had shoved them into an anthill, which I unfortunately knew is a sign of nerve damage.
So I did the standard first responder thing.
I asked myself who I was, where I was, what I was doing, and what just had happened.
Judging by my responses, my level of consciousness was excellent.
And then I wondered if I was bullshitting myself and making things up, but I was pretty sure that my name was Chris Burkhart and I was at a sesshin retreat at Salt Spring Island.
After a short time, I regained the ability to move and did my self-check, and was helped back to the house by my friends.
During the next minutes, I watched my ability shrinking and my dizziness and headache increase as my brain was swelling.
I was very fortunate one of the people present was a former emergency room nurse, and another retreat participant who was expected back on the next morning was a doctor.

In the meantime, I was huddled under a blanket, the slightest motion bringing waves of nausea, as we discussed the options and risks of transport, which meant a vehicle to the helicopter, a helicopter evacuation to Vancouver or Victoria.
And we also talked about brain hemorrhages.
I had taken a lot of first aid and first responder courses, so I was a somewhat confused but active participant in the conversation.
I decided not to be evacuated.
It just did not feel right.
The benefit of not moving felt greater than the higher degree of medical care.
I also thought about a slow leak in my brain or something about not being able to take the pressure, and then I might be dead the next morning.
I was breathing through this koan:
*Should I call my partner veg?
Was there anything I needed to do or say?*
I realized that I had shared my feelings and love all these years.
I was who I was, and that who had expressed itself in my actions.
These are just way much more than words.
Nothing either one of us could say would make any difference.
So I did not call.
I spent the night trying not to move, nausea on one side, headache on the other.
And I was holding a mala in my hand.
Seeing this moment, this breath, this moment, this breath, this moment, this breath.
Falling on my head really did something nice for my meditation.
This moment, this breath, this moment, this breath.
Well, I was still alive the next morning, but I realized I was no longer in any condition that would allow me to make good decisions.
So I handed over all responsibility and went back to sleep.
The doctor at the retreat, the nurse, my host went forth, made telephone calls, held up a ferry, and I found myself being transported back to the mainland.
I was overwhelmed by everybody's kindness.
My partner picked me up at the Savasana ferry, and we drove straight to the emergency room at Saint Joe's.
During the five, six hours I was waiting, I was Avalokiteshvara.
I saw myself surrounded by suffering and I blessed everybody.
Aside from interludes such as emergency rooms, CAT scans, doctor visits, for the next week I just slept.
Oh, and I could not walk without holding on to something.
Turning my head brought on violent bouts of nausea, life at its finest and most interesting.
I admit to frustration over not remembering stuff.
Like the street I lived on, names, concepts, labels were and remain pretty difficult.
Still, somehow I had gone through this whole event without anger or blaming or even without being really upset.
Some folks thought I should take legal action against the owner of the dog, but how could I?
My very good friend Shantideva said, *Their weapons and my body, both are causes of my suffering.
They their weapons true, while I held out my body.
Who then is more worthy of my anger?*
*This human form is like a running sore, merely touched, I cannot stand the pain.
I'm the one who clings to it with blind attachment.
Whom should I resent when pain occurs?*
So let me paraphrase Shantideva a little bit.
The ground and my body, both are causes of my suffering.
The ground offered its hardness, while I offered my head.
Who then is more worthy of my anger?
During the following days, I was slowly getting better, but my decision-making was still significantly impaired.
And my calendar said that I had committed to being on an interfaith panel at Gadget County College.
I briefly reached out, couldn't find anybody to take it on.
So I called the organizers and I told them what happened, and I asked them if they wanted me in my impaired condition.
They said sure.
I persuaded my partner to drive me to Mount Vernon.
At the college, I headed straight for the room where the panel was going to be, found a chair, sat down, did not move.
After some time, the room actually stopped spinning.
Great.
This year, the panel was very small: a Christian pastor, an atheist, and me.
Last year's panel was a lot larger, but a lot of people had accidents, were stuck in traffic, called in, "we can't make it."
So I hope that I spoke well and made some sense because I frankly don't remember.
The questions were the same as the year before and so on.
So my headache, I held a check for some Advils, but it began to reinsert itself after about an hour.
But I was hanging in there, and then came the closing statement by each person.
And that kind of bowed me over.

The pastor made an impassioned plea that anybody who had not chosen Jesus Christ as their personal savior should choose to do so now, because the second coming of Christ was coming and it could happen at any moment.
And that those who do not have Jesus Christ in their lives will suffer terribly.
She was sure that anyone who sincerely now chose Jesus would be forgiven their sins, and when the second coming was going to happen, they would rise to the heavens.
And because, the pastor said, because she loved us all, she wanted us to make every attempt to seek Jesus, because otherwise the consequences would be terrible.
I admit my headache was pretty bad by now, and I really could not think too straight.
But I was thinking, what about those people left behind?
In case you don't know the second coming, Jesus will appear and people who deserve it are going to go straight to heaven.
The rest are going to stay behind and have terribly tortured short lives.
At least that's what I recall.
I have some quotes that I can share, but they're really not that uplifting.
So I wasn't thinking too straight.
And usually when I'm in panels, I really kind of like hold back and give other people room to make their statements, and I didn't know what to say.
However, as shoesaw, I had learned that when my heart is full, I just need to open my mouth and something will come out.
So that's what I did.
I expressed my appreciation for her concern and that I appreciated her sincere efforts.
And I really appreciated what she said, because she made my answer obvious and clear to me.
If there are those who are left behind, who will suffer, who will be tortured, I will be a Bodhisattva.
I will stay behind.
I will stay behind to support every being.
I'm radically a part of those left behind, just in the same way as I'm radically a part of those who go to the heavens.
And once all beings were safe, the Bodhisattvas can go too.
I will stay behind.
I will offer myself, my merit, my effort.
Samantabhadras, enlightening activity to save all beings.
As Mahayana Buddhists, we do uphold the Bodhisattva vows that we chanted again tonight.
*Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.* This is what I said at the interfaith panel.
Thus did I commit and bind myself to the vow of Chiso Bodhisattva.
Chiso Bodhisattva protects travelers, women, children, firemen.
He also protects those who travel from one life to the next.
Chiso is the Bodhisattva of hell beings, having vowed not to enter Nirvana until the hell realm is empty in one of his lives.
He was a girl at that time.
Chiso had cleansed countless beings tortured in the hell realm, and she vowed to free them all.
If I do not go to the hell to help the suffering beings there, who else will go?
I will not become a Buddha until the hells are empty.
Only when all beings have been saved will I enter Nirvana.
In my practice I have been told, and I agree, there is no time.
There is no time.
Death can call us at the most unexpected moment.
How will we meet death?
To me the question seems to be very simple: Did I love enough?
Did I live fully?
Did I learn how to let go?
There is no time, and there never has been time.
I need to say now.
And I have learned that there are two kinds of knowing.
One that loses street names, people names, that does not remember, that asks, "have I told you already?" dot dot dot, and I do not remember again.
One that now really sucks at logic puzzles, that has problems stringing three coherent thoughts together, that does not know the heart sutra and metta sutra by heart any longer.
I watch a me who feels diminished and scared.
I have never been eloquent, and I am more awkward now.
I continue to stumble through memory and language.
So please, don't hold it against me too much when I don't, but let me know, it helps.
And there is that other kind of knowing.
A knowing that I'd rather go through the gates of hell to save beings instead of taking the express elevator to the heavens.
A knowing that sees each and everyone here like shining jewels, interconnected throughout this life and all lives to come.
And I am happy.
There is a knowing of the metta sutra that holds the heart while language does not hit the right word.
And I am happy about that too.
And seeing us all holding together intrasnet, how could one even call it martyr to help those who are not chosen to go to heaven?

I realized that while I have had much childhood conditioning around Christianity, having grown up Catholic, baptized at four days old, confirmed, the great surprise looking back was that my refuge did not go back to my childhood conditioning.
My refuge was my breath.
And this moment, and this moment, when I was waiting through that night,
did I love enough?
Did I live fully?
Did I learn how to let go?
In this spirit, I would like to say that those I have caused offense or pain, I am sorry.
Often there are misunderstandings or a point is not made well.
Something is said badly.
A choke goes awry.
In that case, please let us speak about it because there is no time.
I vow to enter them.
It is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.
